newsitem.title: UK: Swoop on alleged war criminals a start-UK minister.
newsitem.headline: Swoop on alleged war criminals a start-UK minister.

text.p: Thursday's dramatic swoop on two alleged war criminals in Bosnia by British special forces signalled stronger international determination to bring such people to trial, Britain said on Sunday.

"This was a signal. This was a start. These people have got to face justice, and we are determined internationally that they are going do to so," Defence Secretary George Robertson said in a BBC television interview.

British troops in the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia shot dead Simo Drljaca, former police chief in the town of Prijedor, on Thursday after he tried to avoid arrest by firing on them. One soldier suffered a leg wound.

The troops also arrested the director of Prijedor hospital, Milan Kovacevic, wanted for complicity in genocide against Bosnian Moslems and Croats during the war. Kovacevic is now jailed in The Hague awaiting trial.

French Defence Minister Alain Richard, on a visit to French peacekeepers in Sarajevo, defended the Prijedor arrests against Russian criticism and said no means could be spared to enforce the rule of international law.
"France, which is one of the countries which created international law...cannot disdain the means which can enable this international justice to be enforce," he said.
"I don't think there is a difference of principle with Russia on this issue," Richard told reporters in remarks broadcast by France 3 television.

"There is political coordination among the powers which have responsibility here (in Bosnia) to obtain the best possible results on the warrants handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal (in The Hague)," he said.

Robertson said the Prijedor episode reflected increasing impatience among the 34 nations involved in SFOR at the failure of Bosnian state authorities to live up to their undertakings in the Dayton peace treaty.

"They said they would do certain things, they are simply not doing them. And one of the things they are not doing is bringing to book those who have been accused in the international court of these terrible crimes."
In this context, he said, the Prijedor raids were "an important signal of the resolution not just of this government but of the world community in general".

He pointed to the arrest two weeks ago of the former Serb mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic, in connection with the massacre of 260 Croat hospital patients as another sign the world community was getting tough.
"I think that not just in Britain but elsewhere there is an increasing determination," Robertson said.
He declined to speculate on further operations by SFOR troops against those indicted on war crimes charges.
Seventy-six people have been publicly indicted by the tribunal, the majority of them Serbs including their former wartime president, Radovan Karadzic, and army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
Asked about reports that Karadzic had forsaken his headquarters in Pale, outside Sarajevo, and fled to the neighbouring republic of Montenegro, Robertson said:
"This (the Prijedor incident) will have upset a lot of people who thought they were getting away with it."
"What has happened this week is going to make them less easy in their beds and some of them will do rash things, which may well have further consequences."
